resources.string: European beech
Fagus sylvatica
Hêtre commun
Smooth grey bark. Young leaf margins are hairy, scarcely toothed or untoothed; buds are long and pointed. Triangular beechnuts in a bristly cup.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European hornbeam
Carpinus betulus
Charme commun

Doubly toothed leaves with prominent lateral veins. Buds lie against the twig. The small dry fruit is a ribbed nutlet carried by a large three-lobed bract. The winglike organ is this supporting bract, separate from the fruit wall.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Field maple
Acer campestre
Érable champêtre
Small leaves with five rather rounded lobes. Twigs sometimes bear corky ridges. The two samara wings spread widely, nearly in a straight line.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common ash
Fraxinus excelsior
Frêne commun
Black buds and opposite leaves, usually with 7–13 toothed leaflets. Flowers lack petals and appear before the leaves. Elongated winged dry fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sweet chestnut
Castanea sativa
Châtaignier commun
Long simple leaves with sharp teeth. Long upright catkins. Burr densely covered in slender spines, usually enclosing several chestnuts.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common hazel
Corylus avellana
Noisetier commun
Often has several stems from the base. Broad hairy leaves with a heart-shaped base. Male catkins in winter; tiny female flowers with red stigmas. Nuts in leafy husks.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common hawthorn
Crataegus monogyna
Aubépine monogyne
Thorny twigs. Deeply lobed leaves; small five-petalled flowers usually have one style. Red fruits usually contain one stone; hybridisation with other hawthorns occurs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common dogwood
Cornus sanguinea
Cornouiller sanguin
Opposite leaves with lateral veins curving towards the tip. Young twigs often red. White four-petalled flowers and black fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European spindle
Euonymus europaeus
Fusain d’Europe
Opposite finely toothed leaves; green, sometimes angular twigs. Small four-petalled flowers. Pink four-lobed capsules reveal bright orange seed coverings.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common broom
Cytisus scoparius
Genêt à balais
Green angled stems without spines. Lower leaves often have three leaflets, upper leaves are simple; some fall early. Large yellow flowers and dark pods with hairy margins.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common heather
Calluna vulgaris
Callune commune
Tiny opposite scale-like leaves in four rows. Small pink flowers with four coloured sepals longer than the corolla. A dwarf shrub of acid soils.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Bell heather
Erica cinerea
Bruyère cendrée
Small narrow leaves in whorls of three. Purple-pink urn-shaped corolla with four small lobes. Unlike the scale-leaved common heather.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Brown knapweed
Centaurea jacea
Centaurée jacée
Purple heads of tubular florets, often enlarged around the edge. Involucral bracts have brown fringed appendages. Variable and similar to other knapweeds.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Lesser celandine
Ficaria verna
Ranunculus ficaria; ficaire
Shiny heart-shaped leaves, sometimes dark-marked. Spring flowers usually have 8–12 narrow petals and three sepals. Foliage usually disappears after spring.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common foxglove
Digitalis purpurea
Digitale pourpre
A large rosette precedes the leafy stem. Long raceme of hanging tubular flowers, often facing one side; spotted inside. Capsules hold numerous tiny seeds.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Harebell
Campanula rotundifolia
Campanule à feuilles rondes
Rounded basal leaves often disappear by flowering; stem leaves are narrow and elongated. Blue five-lobed bell flowers. Look for both leaf types.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Wild carrot
Daucus carota
Carotte sauvage
Stem and leaves usually hairy; leaves finely divided. Umbels have divided bracts, sometimes a dark central flower. Rays often curl into a nest at maturity.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cock’s-foot
Dactylis glomerata
Dactyle aggloméré
Tufted grass; young leaves are folded and sheaths flattened. Panicle has dense spikelet clusters, often facing one side. A membranous ligule is visible.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cornus mas
Cornelian cherry
Cornelier; cornier; cornelian cherry
Small yellow umbels appear before the leaves. Opposite, entire leaves have curved lateral veins. Elongated red drupes contain a hard stone. Unlike common dogwood, its flowers are yellow.
Open woods, hedges and limestone slopes; also cultivated.
Crataegus laevigata
Midland hawthorn
Épine blanche; aubépine épineuse; Crataegus oxyacantha
Leaves are shallowly lobed, mainly in their upper half. Flowers usually have two styles, sometimes three; fruits normally contain two stones. Hybridisation with common hawthorn is frequent.
Hedges and woods, especially in cooler temperate parts of France.
Frangula alnus
Alder buckthorn
Rhamnus frangula; aulne noir; alder buckthorn
A thornless shrub with alternate, entire leaves and curved lateral veins. Tiny greenish five-parted flowers sit in leaf axils. Drupes turn red and then black; twigs have pale lenticels.
Damp woods and heaths, often on acidic soils; widespread outside the driest districts.
Genista tinctoria
Dyer’s greenweed
Herbe à jaunir; dyers greenweed
A thornless small shrub with simple lanceolate leaves. Yellow pea flowers cluster at shoot tips, followed by elongated pods. Unlike broom, its leaves remain simple.
Heaths, nutrient-poor grassland and sunny woodland edges across much of France.
Cichorium intybus
Chicory
Barbe de capucin; chicory

Stiff branching stems rise above divided basal leaves; upper leaves are smaller. Blue heads consist entirely of five-toothed strap-shaped florets. Short fruits carry minute scales, without a large feathery parachute.
Road verges, tracksides and dry grasslands; widespread.
Cardamine pratensis
Cuckooflower
Cressonnette; cresson des prés; lady’s smock

Basal leaves have fairly rounded leaflets, while stem leaflets are narrow. Pale flowers have four petals and six stamens, two shorter than the others. Long siliques open by two valves to release the seeds.
Damp meadows, ditches and stream margins, from lowlands to mountains.
Capsella bursa-pastoris
Shepherd’s purse
Bourse à pasteur; shepherds purse
Rosette leaves vary from entire to deeply divided; stem leaves clasp the stem. Tiny white flowers have four petals. The lengthening raceme bears triangular, inverted heart-shaped silicles.
Gardens, fields, pavements and disturbed ground throughout France; may flower nearly year-round in mild weather.
Geranium robertianum
Herb-robert
Herbe à Robert; bec de grue; herb Robert
Often reddish, hairy stems carry leaves deeply divided into three to five further-cut segments. Five-petalled pink flowers usually occur in pairs. The fruit has a long beak above five mericarps.
Woods, old walls, banks and shady gardens; very widespread.
Apple-ring acacia
Acacia albida · kad · cad · gao

Large tree with pale young twigs and paired straight stipular thorns. Bipinnate leaves and slender creamy flower spikes. Thick orange-brown pods curl into open rings. Its often reversed leaf cycle is particularly distinctive.
Widespread through African savannas, alluvial plains and seasonal watercourses; frequently retained in cultivated fields.
Sodom apple
Calotrope · arbre à soie · Sodom apple
Upright shrub with thick, nearly stalkless opposite leaves and milky latex. The waxy five-lobed corolla surrounds a five-parted corona. Inflated follicles release flat seeds with silky tufts.
Dry northern and tropical Africa, especially sandy disturbed ground, roadsides and overgrazed areas; also native in southwestern Asia.
Guiera
Nguer · guier · n’guère

Much-branched shrub with small grey-green, softly hairy leaves, usually opposite. Cream flower heads have projecting stamens. Long spindle-shaped silky fruits radiate from the same head, producing a distinctive spider-like cluster.
Savannas from Senegal to Sudan. Often abundant on sandy soils and degraded fallows in the Sahelian and Sudanian zones.
Kinkeliba
Kinkeliba · quinquéliba · Combretum raimbaultii
Spreading shrub, sometimes a small tree or scrambling climber. Opposite leaves become reddish-brown when old. Small white flowers occur in short spikes; the dry reddish fruit has four papery wings.
West Africa to the Central African Republic, in savanna scrub, rocky sites and woodland margins. The illustrated habit is shrubby.
Buffel grass
Pennisetum ciliare · buffel grass

Tufted perennial grass with narrow blades. Its dense false spike is purple when young, becoming straw-coloured. Bristles surround groups of spikelets and remain with the dispersal unit. The true fruit is a small caryopsis.
Common in warm dry parts of Africa, especially open sandy habitats; also planted as pasture and present outside Africa.
Common thatching grass
Hyparrhénie hérissée · chaume · thatching grass

Dense perennial tussock with wiry culms. The inflorescence branches into pairs of hairy racemes, each pair accompanied by a spatheole. Long bent awns extend from fertile spikelets; they are not petals.
Widespread in African grasslands and open disturbed sites, particularly familiar in southern Africa; also native in the Mediterranean and southwestern Asia.
Flower-of-an-hour
Hibiscus d’Afrique · ketmie d’Afrique · bladder hibiscus

Hairy annual with deeply divided leaves. Pale yellow petals have a dark purple base around the staminal column. A papery inflated, prominently veined calyx encloses the five-valved capsule. Flowers are short-lived.
Fields and disturbed open habitats. Native in the Mediterranean and parts of Eurasia; naturalized in much of eastern and southern Africa.
Faidherbia albida
Calotropis procera
Guiera senegalensis
Combretum micranthum
Cenchrus ciliaris
Hyparrhenia hirta
Hibiscus trionum
Red-osier dogwood
Cornus stolonifera; red-twig dogwood; cornouiller à bois rouge
Suckering shrub whose young twigs turn conspicuously red, especially in winter. Opposite leaves have arched veins. Flat clusters of four-petalled cream flowers produce white to bluish drupes.
Widespread in northern and western North America and parts of the eastern United States, especially along streams and wetlands.
Cornus sericea
Purple coneflower
Eastern purple coneflower; rudbeckie pourpre

Perennial with rough, often three-veined leaves. Pink-purple ray florets spread or droop around a prominent spiny orange-brown cone of disc florets. The dry fruits are short angular cypselae, without a feathery pappus.
Central and eastern United States, in open woods and prairie margins. Widely cultivated, with many horticultural forms.
Echinacea purpurea
Common sunflower
Sunflower; grand soleil; hélianthe annuel

Tall rough annual. Lower leaves are opposite, upper leaves alternate, with three main veins. Wild plants are often branched with several heads, unlike many giant single-headed crop forms. Each head combines yellow ray florets and fertile disc florets; the “seeds” are cypselae.
Native to North America, especially central and western regions. Domesticated there and now cultivated and naturalized worldwide.
Helianthus annuus
California poppy
California poppy; eschscholzie

Annual or short-lived perennial with finely divided blue-green foliage. Four silky orange to yellow petals form a cup above a small receptacular rim; the fused sepals fall as a cap. Long slender capsules split into two valves.
Western North America, including California and adjacent regions of the United States and Mexico. Widely introduced as an ornamental.
Eschscholzia californica
Pepper and chilli
Capsicum annuum
Poivron · Piment · Bell pepper · Chili pepper

Branching herb or short-lived subshrub with simple, usually entire leaves. Flowers are commonly solitary at the nodes; their white corolla usually has five lobes, though lobe number and colour vary. The stamens have distinct anthers around the style, unlike the conspicuous yellow Solanum cone. The fruit is a berry with a persistent cup-like calyx. In a bell pepper, a fleshy wall surrounds large cavities and pale placental tissue carrying flattened seeds. Sweet peppers and many hot chillies belong to this same species.

American domesticated species cultivated worldwide in warm conditions. Perennial where frost and other conditions permit, but usually grown as a seasonal crop in temperate regions. The plate shows a red bell-pepper form; slender, upright and differently coloured fruits also occur.
Forking leafy stems, solitary flowers and hanging berries; a bell-pepper cultivar is represented.
Simple oval leaf with pointed tip, entire margin and branching lateral veins; leaves are borne alternately on the side shoot.
Five-lobed white fused corolla with separate grey-violet anthers and a central green style. Lobe number and colour can vary.
Main subject: fleshy bell-pepper berry with calyx and stalk. The longitudinal section exposes a cavity and pale seed-bearing placenta.
Arabica coffee
coffee arabica coffee bean

Evergreen shrub or small tree with nearly horizontal lateral branches. Glossy, wavy, opposite leaves have stipules between their petioles. White flowers, usually five-lobed, cluster in the axils. The red fruit normally contains two seeds: coffee beans. This drupe is commonly called a coffee cherry.
Native to eastern Africa; cultivated in tropical regions, often at elevation.
Upright axis and tiered lateral branches with paired leaves.
Curving veins, wavy edge; stipule between two petioles in inset.
Five lobes, five stamens and bifid stigma; floral tube in side view.
Red fruit, section with two seeds and unroasted bean with ventral groove.
Pummelo
pomelo shaddock Citrus grandis Citrus decumana

Evergreen tree with large leaves and conspicuously winged petioles. Thick white flowers bear many stamens. The pummelo is a hesperidium, a specialized berry with thick rind and segments filled with juice vesicles. Citrus maxima is distinct from the hybrid grapefruit, Citrus × paradisi.
Native to tropical Asia; cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
Dense evergreen crown; representative adult tree habit.
Large blade with a rounded tip, glandular dots and broadly winged petiole.
Five thick petals, stamens joined basally in small bundles and rounded central stigma.
Fruit and section: rind, thick white layer and juice-filled segments.
Coffea arabica
Citrus maxima
Cucumber
cucumber gherkin Cucumis sativus

Annual trailing or climbing herb with simple tendrils and rough, palmately veined leaves. Yellow flowers are usually male or female; the female flower has an inferior ovary already resembling a tiny cucumber. The fruit is a pepo, a specialized berry. It is usually harvested green and immature; some cultivars produce fruit without fertilization.
Asian origin, cultivated worldwide. Height depends on support; the plate shows a trained vine and a seeded fruit.
Trained stem, alternate leaves and tendrils; the support is not part of the plant.
Shallowly five-lobed blade, cordate base, palmate veins and tendril inset.
Five-lobed female flower with three-lobed stigma; inferior ovary in side view.
Immature green fruit, yellowing ripe fruit and section with three placental regions.
Soybean
soy soybean soya edamame Glycine max

Hairy annual herb with leaves usually divided into three leaflets. Small white to violet pea flowers arise in leaf axils. Hairy pods contain several seeds, used for protein and oil; immature seeds are eaten as edamame. The plate shows a violet-flowered, yellow-seeded form.
Domesticated in eastern Asia and cultivated worldwide.
Upright stems, trifoliolate leaves and axillary pods.
Three entire, veined, hairy leaflets; seedling detail shows opposite simple first leaves above the cotyledons.
Standard, wings and keel; small axillary raceme inset.
Hairy pod and opened valve with three seeds; visible hilum.
Cucumis sativus
Glycine max
Camellia sinensis
Tea plant
tea green black oolong Camellia sinensis

Evergreen shrub with alternate, leathery, finely toothed leaves. White flowers have six to eight petals, many stamens and a divided style. Capsules contain large brown seeds. Buds and young leaves provide tea; processing helps distinguish green tea from black tea.
Asian origins; long cultivation obscures the wild range. Grown in many mild, humid regions, often pruned low for harvesting.
Freely branching habit; plantation pruning produces a lower crown.
Toothed leaf and lateral veins; inset shows a harvestable shoot with a terminal bud.
Seven petals shown, numerous stamens and a three-branched style; axillary flower inset.
Closed and open capsule with brown seeds; the number of developed chambers varies.
Gossypium hirsutum
Upland cotton
cotton upland Mexican cotton textile fibre Gossypium hirsutum

Branching perennial usually cultivated as an annual. Leaves have three to five palmate lobes. Three large, cut-edged bracts surround each five-petalled flower; the stamens form a column. Ripe capsules split into valves, exposing seeds clothed in long hairs: these fibres are cotton.
Native to tropical America, including the Caribbean region. Widely cultivated in warm countries for textile fibre.
Branching stem with alternate leaves, flowers and capsules at different stages.
Five-lobed blade with a heart-shaped base, palmate veins and a long petiole.
Five cream petals, a staminal column and three toothed bracts; side-view inset.
Green capsule and four open valves; fibres grow on the seeds, shown separately in detail.
Caraway
Carum carvi
Caraway Carum carvi
Usually biennial herb. Aromatic fruits are commonly called caraway seeds.
Temperate Eurasia; cultivated and naturalized elsewhere.
Rosette and upright branched stems.
Finely divided leaf with narrow segments.
Compound umbels of small white, sometimes pinkish flowers.
Two narrow ribbed mericarps, shown enlarged.
Barley
Hordeum vulgare
Barley Hordeum vulgare
Annual cereal with three spikelets at each rachis node. Their fertility distinguishes two-row and six-row barley.
Domesticated in the Middle East; cultivated worldwide.
Tufted culms and usually long-awned spikes.
Strap-shaped leaf, sheath and clasping auricles.
Awned spike; petal-free floret with three stamens.
Caryopsis; diagrammatic mature spike, here representing six-row barley.
Chickpea
Cicer arietinum
Chickpea Cicer arietinum
Glandular annual. The leaf ends in a leaflet, without a terminal tendril.
Domesticated plant widely cultivated for its seeds.
Branched stems with small compound leaves.
Toothed leaflets and terminal leaflet.
Pea-shaped flowers, solitary or paired, white to purplish.
Hairy inflated pod, here opened around two seeds; seed count varies.
Melon
Cucumis melo
Melon Cucumis melo
Tendril-bearing creeping herb. The fruit is a pepo; shape, rind and flesh vary among cultivars.
African and Asian origin; cultivated worldwide.
Creeping stems with large leaves.
Rounded lobed leaf with palmate veins.
Yellow male flower and smaller female flower with an inferior ovary; other cultivars may bear bisexual flowers.
Rounded pepo; section showing central cavity and seeds.
Coconut palm
Cocos nucifera
Cocos nucifera

A palm with an unbranched ring-scarred stem and long pinnate fronds. Male and female flowers occur on the same plant. The coconut is a fibrous drupe: its husk surrounds a hard endocarp enclosing one seed. The white flesh is endosperm.
Grown throughout tropical coasts and islands; ancient transport complicates the original range.
Ring-scarred stipe, arching fronds and fruits below the crown.
Many narrow leaflets share one frond rachis.
Larger basal female flowers and smaller distal male flowers.
Whole drupe and section: fibrous husk, shell, white endosperm and cavity.
Natal lily
Clivia miniata
Clivia miniata

An evergreen rhizomatous herb without an onion-like bulb. Strap-shaped leaves make a two-ranked fan. A leafless scape bears an umbel of orange funnel-shaped six-tepalled flowers, followed by berries ripening red.
Native to southern African woodland and widely grown as an ornamental; flower colour varies among selections.
Two-ranked leaf fan and elevated umbel; no onion bulb.
Strap leaf with parallel veins and a blunt tip.
Funnel with six tepals and six stamens; umbel inset.
Red berries borne on the former umbel.
Lily of the valley
Convallaria majalis
Convallaria majalis

A rhizomatous woodland perennial, usually with two broad basal leaves. One-sided racemes bear nodding bells with six fused tepals ending in recurved lobes. Red berries may follow. The whole plant is toxic; these plates describe morphology.
Native to Eurasia; cultivated and naturalized elsewhere. Rhizomes form spreading patches.
Paired basal leaves and one-sided raceme above a rhizome.
Broad elliptic leaf with curved parallel veins.
Nodding six-lobed bell and enlarged six-part end view.
Small red berries on the former one-sided raceme.
Common fig
Ficus carica
Ficus carica

The fig is a syconium: a hollow fleshy receptacle with many tiny flowers on its inner surface, connected outside by an ostiole. Grainlike structures inside the mature fig are individual fruits. Some cultivated forms set fruit without pollination; requirements vary among fig types.
Mediterranean and western Asian origins; widely cultivated, with variable fruit colour and leaf lobing.
Low spreading tree with palmately lobed leaves.
Broad blade with three to five major lobes and palmate veins.
Cut young syconium: flowers face the cavity, beneath the apical ostiole.
Fig section showing individual fruit units within the fleshy receptacle.
Turkish hazel
Corylus colurna
Corylus colurna

A tree-form hazel rather than a many-stemmed shrub. Pendant male catkins and small female flowers occur on the same tree. Nut clusters are surrounded by deeply divided hairy involucres: these leafy envelopes are distinct from the hard nut wall.
Southeastern Europe and western Asia; widely planted as an ornamental tree.
Single trunk with a conical to rounded deciduous crown.
Heart-based blade with double teeth and pinnate veins.
Male catkins and tiny female bud with red stigmas.
Clustered nuts with long divided involucre lobes.
Large yellow foxglove
Digitalis grandiflora
Digitalis grandiflora

A perennial foxglove with creamy-yellow tubular bells, generally arranged on one side of the raceme. The throat bears darker markings and the flower has four stamens. The ovoid dry capsule opens by two valves, releasing numerous small seeds. The plant is toxic if eaten.
Europe to western Siberia; also cultivated. Foliage may persist through winter in suitable conditions.
Basal leaves and a mostly unbranched one-sided flowering stem.
Toothed lanceolate blade with pinnate veins.
Yellow tubular corolla with a marked throat and hanging orientation.
Ovoid capsule containing numerous small seeds.
Cornflower
Centaurea cyanus
Centaurea cyanus

An annual with narrow upper leaves and blue flower heads. Enlarged sterile peripheral florets form funnels, not the flat ray petals of a daisy; the central florets are fertile. Each one-seeded fruit has a short bristly pappus. Cultivated colours vary.
European origins; spread with arable cultivation and planted as an ornamental.
Branched leafy annual with terminal flower heads.
Narrow upper leaf with fine hairs; lower leaves may be lobed.
Sterile outer funnel florets around fertile tubular florets and an involucre.
One-seeded fruit topped by a short bristly pappus.
Dropwort
Filipendula vulgaris
Filipendula vulgaris

A perennial rosaceous herb with finely lobed pinnate leaves and a branched inflorescence. White flowers often have six petals, with variable counts, and many stamens. Separate carpels mature into a cluster of hairy achenes. Swollen root portions store reserves; they are not fruits.
Europe to southwestern Siberia and northern Africa; dry grasslands and cultivated plantings, with introductions elsewhere.
Basal pinnate foliage and a branched flowering axis.
Pinnate leaf with many lobed leaflets.
Branched white-flowered inflorescence; petal number varies.
Separate hairy achenes clustered on the enlarged receptacle.
Northern water hemlock
Cicuta virosa
cowbane; water hemlock

Highly poisonous wetland perennial with a smooth hollow stem, finely divided toothed leaves and compound white umbels. The short rhizome has chambered pith and fibrous or tuberous roots. Every part is dangerous; resemblance to edible Apiaceae makes casual identification unsafe.
Subarctic and temperate Northern Hemisphere; marshes, fens and wet margins.
Erect marsh herb with divided leaves and terminal white umbels.
Pinnate leaf with narrow sharply toothed leaflets.
Small white flowers grouped in compound umbels.
Paired mericarps and the chambered rhizome shown separately; all parts are poisonous.
Quinoa
Chenopodium quinoa
quinua; goosefoot quinoa

Andean annual pseudocereal in Amaranthaceae, not a grass. Alternate leaves are often broad and toothed below, narrower above; tiny flowers form dense terminal and lateral panicles. The small seeds are eaten as grain, and cultivar colours vary.
Native to the Andes from Ecuador to northwestern Argentina; now cultivated worldwide.
Upright annual with branching terminal panicles.
Broad lower leaf with an angular, sometimes toothed outline.
Minute flowers crowded into dense branched clusters.
Tiny seed-bearing fruitlets; edible seeds are pseudocereal grain, not grass caryopses.
Robusta coffee
Coffea canephora
robusta; canephora coffee

Evergreen tropical shrub or small tree with opposite glossy leaves, interpetiolar stipules and small white flowers in axillary clusters. The red drupes usually contain two seeds. Robusta is a cultivated coffee type associated mainly with this species.
Tropical western and central Africa; cultivated throughout the tropics.
Evergreen shrub or small tree with opposite, tiered branches.
Opposite elliptic leaves with wavy margins and a stipule between petioles.
White tubular flowers clustered near leaf axils.
Red drupe with two coffee seeds.
Liberica coffee
Coffea liberica
Liberian coffee

Evergreen coffee tree with notably large, leathery elliptic leaves and wavy margins. White fragrant flowers form axillary clusters; the comparatively large cherry-like drupe usually contains two seeds. Leaf and fruit size vary, so these traits alone do not identify every cultivated coffee.
Native to western tropical Africa; cultivated in tropical Africa and Southeast Asia.
Evergreen tree with large leaves and axillary flowering clusters.
Large leathery elliptic leaf with a wavy edge and raised veins.
Fragrant white star-like flowers in axillary clusters.
Large red coffee drupe opened to show its two seeds.
Maidenhair tree
Ginkgo biloba
ginkgo; maidenhair tree

Deciduous, usually dioecious gymnosperm with long shoots and short shoots bearing fan-shaped leaves with repeatedly forked veins. Male trees bear pollen catkins; female trees develop naked seeds with a fleshy outer seed coat, not a true fruit. Seeds can be toxic unless properly prepared.
Native to China; widely planted as an ornamental tree in temperate regions.
Deciduous tree with irregular branches and leaf clusters on short shoots.
Fan-shaped, often two-lobed leaf with repeatedly forked veins.
Pollen-bearing male catkin; male and female structures occur on separate trees.
Female naked seed with fleshy seed coat; it is not a fruit, and raw seeds can be toxic.
Hemp
Cannabis sativa
hemp; cannabis

Annual herb with angular stems and palmately divided leaves bearing narrow, coarsely toothed leaflets. Plants are commonly male or female, though forms with both sexes occur. Female flowers are compact; male flowers form looser panicles. The fruit is a small achene.
Native range in Central Asia to Xinjiang and Pakistan; cultivated and naturalized widely.
Tall annual herb with an upright, branching leafy stem.
Palmately divided leaf with narrow, sharply toothed leaflets.
Compact female flower cluster; sexes usually occur on separate plants.
Small hard achene with a mottled, reticulate surface.
Papaya
Carica papaya
papaw; pawpaw (tropical papaya)

Soft-wooded tropical tree, often with a single unbranched trunk crowned by very large palmately lobed leaves. Flowers may be male, female or bisexual depending on plant and cultivar. The fleshy berry carries many black seeds in a central cavity.
Native from southern Mexico to Venezuela; cultivated throughout the tropics.
Usually one soft, unbranched trunk with a crown of large leaves.
Very large palmately lobed leaf on a long petiole.
Pale female flower on a short stalk; flower form varies among plants.
Fleshy berry, shown cut lengthwise with many seeds in its central cavity.
Greater celandine
Chelidonium majus
greater celandine; tetterwort

Perennial woodland herb with blue-green pinnatifid leaves and clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers. Broken stems exude conspicuous orange latex. The plant is toxic; do not handle the sap or ingest any part.
Native from Macaronesia and Europe to western Siberia, the Mediterranean and northern Iran; introduced elsewhere.
Delicate branching perennial of shaded woods and disturbed ground.
Blue-green leaf divided into rounded pinnate lobes.
Small bright-yellow flower with four petals and many stamens.
Long narrow capsule; cut stems exude orange latex.
Lemongrass
Cymbopogon citratus
lemongrass; lemon grass; citronnelle

Clump-forming aromatic perennial grass grown for its lemon-scented leaves and pale lower sheaths used in cooking and drinks. Do not confuse it with citronella grass, Cymbopogon nardus, a related species.
Native range given by Kew as southern India and Sri Lanka; cultivated throughout the tropics.
Dense evergreen clump of tall grass with overlapping pale leaf sheaths.
Long narrow, aromatic, parallel-veined leaf blade.
Loose drooping branched panicle, rarely seen on cultivated plants.
Small grain, as in other grasses.
Rocoto pepper
Capsicum pubescens
Rocoto; manzano pepper

Perennial pepper often grown as a branching shrub. The species is characterized by pubescent stems and leaves, purple flowers with purple anthers, and dark seeds. Ripe fruit colour and shape vary among cultivars.
Native to the Andes of Peru and Bolivia; cultivated elsewhere in cool highland climates.
Branching, often woody-based perennial pepper shrub.
Broad ovate leaf with a soft covering of hairs.
Purple corolla and purple anthers distinguish the flowers.
Variable rounded or elongated peppers; the seeds are dark when mature.
Spear thistle
Cirsium vulgare
Spear thistle; bull thistle

Biennial thistle with deeply lobed prickly leaves and stems bearing discontinuous spiny wings that descend from the leaves. Purple flower heads have narrow spine-tipped bracts; fruits carry a feathery pappus.
Native from Europe and northwestern Africa through temperate Asia; introduced widely.
Branched biennial stem with spiny leaf wings and several purple heads.
Deeply divided leaf with sharp spines along the lobes and margins.
Purple florets rise above dense, spine-tipped involucral bracts.
Achene with a feathery pappus for wind dispersal.
Round-leaved sundew
Drosera rotundifolia
Round-leaved sundew; common sundew

Tiny carnivorous perennial of nutrient-poor bogs. A basal rosette of round leaves bears red gland-tipped tentacles with sticky mucilage that traps small insects. A slender leafless scape carries a one-sided raceme of small white or pink flowers.
Native across temperate and subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere and a few areas farther south.
Very small basal rosette with a slender flower stalk rising above it.
Round leaf covered in red glandular tentacles tipped with sticky droplets.
Small white to pink five-petalled flowers form a one-sided raceme.
Dry capsule releases many tiny seeds after flowering.
Cumin
Cuminum cyminum
Cumin; Roman caraway

Short annual herb of western Asia, cultivated for its aromatic dried fruits used as the spice cumin. It differs from greater ammi in its compact stature, threadlike foliage and narrow, strongly ribbed fruits.
Native from Iraq to Afghanistan; widely cultivated.
Small bushy annual with fine leaves and delicate flower umbels.
Leaves are repeatedly divided into very narrow, threadlike segments.
Small compound umbels carry white to pale pink flowers.
The narrow paired fruits have prominent longitudinal ribs; dried fruits are the cumin spice.
Lierre grimpant
Hedera helix
Lierre commun; English ivy

An evergreen woody climber that attaches to supports by aerial rootlets. Juvenile shoots carry alternate, palmately lobed leaves; flowering adult shoots instead bear unlobed leaves and rounded clusters of small greenish flowers. Blue-black berries mature later. Berries and other parts can cause illness if eaten, so the plant must not be confused with edible climbing plants.
Native from much of Europe and the Mediterranean region eastward to Iran; planted and naturalized elsewhere.
Evergreen climbing or ground-covering woody plant; adult flowering shoots are less clinging and have unlobed leaves.
Juvenile leaves are alternate and palmately lobed; adult flowering shoots have alternate, unlobed leaves.
Small greenish-yellow flowers form dense, rounded umbels in autumn.
Rounded berries ripen dark blue-black; they are not edible and can cause gastrointestinal upset.
Cestre nocturne
Cestrum nocturnum
Cestre nocturne; jasmin de nuit

An evergreen tropical shrub, unrelated to true jasmines. Alternate glossy lance-shaped leaves accompany clusters of slender greenish-white tubular flowers that release a strong fragrance at night. Small pale berries follow. The berries are poisonous; the familiar “night jasmine” name must not be confused with edible jasmines.
Native from Mexico to Venezuela; widely cultivated and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions.
Evergreen, branching shrub, usually 1–3 m tall.
Simple, alternate, glossy lance-shaped leaves with entire margins.
Clusters of long greenish-white tubular flowers open mainly at night and are strongly scented.
Small pale berries follow flowering; they are poisonous and must not be eaten.
Common hop
Humulus lupulus
Common hop; hop

A rough, twining perennial vine arising from a persistent rhizome. Plants are usually male or female; female flowers form papery, cone-like clusters whose aromatic glands are used in brewing. The fruit is a small achene enclosed by the enlarged bracts.
Native from Europe across temperate Asia to Siberia and northern Iran, and in Morocco; cultivated and introduced widely.
Herbaceous perennial climber with annual twining stems that die back to the rhizome.
Opposite, long-stalked leaves are broadly heart-shaped and usually palmately 3–5-lobed with toothed margins.
Male flowers are branched and loose; female flowers are grouped in compact, pendant, cone-like inflorescences.
A small compressed achene develops beneath persistent papery bracts; the cone is not a true cone.
Jerusalem artichoke
Helianthus tuberosus
Jerusalem artichoke; sunroot; sunchoke

A tall perennial sunflower that spreads through underground rhizomes ending in edible tubers. Lower leaves are usually opposite and upper leaves alternate. Yellow heads contain an outer ring of ray florets and a central disc; the tubers are storage stems, not roots.
Native to central and eastern North America; cultivated and naturalised across temperate regions.
Coarse, upright perennial herb, often 1–3 m tall, arising from tuber-bearing rhizomes.
Broad, rough, toothed leaves are opposite below and alternate above, often with a rough underside.
Yellow composite heads have yellow ray florets around a darker disc of many small tubular florets.
The small dry fruit is an achene; edible irregular tubers form underground on rhizomes.
Pink sundew
Drosera capillaris
Pink sundew; dwarf sundew

A tiny carnivorous wetland plant forming a flat rosette of sticky glandular leaves. Insects adhere to the tentacles and contribute nutrients in poor soils. Its small pink, sometimes white, flowers are carried on a separate smooth scape; leaf shape and flower colour help separate it from related sundews.
Native from the southeastern United States through Mexico and the Caribbean to Central and South America.
Very low rosette, generally only a few centimetres across, with a slender upright flowering stalk.
Prostrate spatulate to nearly round blades are covered with red gland-tipped tentacles and sticky mucilage.
A smooth, leafless scape bears several small five-petaled flowers, usually pink and sometimes white.
A small capsule contains minute ridged seeds after the petals fall.
Mandrinette
Hibiscus fragilis
Mandrinette; Mauritius hibiscus

A rare shrub endemic to Mauritius. Like other hibiscus, it has alternate toothed leaves and large five-petaled flowers with a prominent staminal column; its species identity depends on the whole plant and provenance, not flower colour alone. Kew accepts H. fragilis while noting an alternative taxonomic treatment, so the name follows POWO.
Endemic to Mauritius, where remaining wild populations are very restricted; cultivated for conservation.
Woody, branching shrub of seasonally dry tropical slopes.
Simple alternate ovate leaves have toothed margins and tapering tips.
Large solitary five-petaled pink flowers have a central staminal column bearing numerous anthers.
An ovoid five-locular capsule develops after flowering and releases seeds when mature.
Common mare’s-tail
Hippuris vulgaris
Common mare’s-tail; marestail

An aquatic perennial with erect emergent shoots and submerged forms in still or slow-moving freshwater. Numerous narrow leaves occur in close whorls along the stem. The tiny flowers are sessile in leaf axils and lack a perianth, unlike the conspicuous terminal cones of a horsetail (Equisetum).
Native across subarctic and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with scattered southern occurrences.
Rhizomatous aquatic herb rooted in mud; stems may rise above the water or remain submerged.
Narrow simple leaves occur in dense whorls; submerged leaves are softer and more elongated than emergent ones.
Minute sessile flowers sit in the upper leaf axils; they lack petals and sepals and have a single stamen.
A small one-seeded nut-like fruit develops in the leaf axil.
Umbrella papyrus
Cyperus alternifolius
Umbrella papyrus; umbrella sedge

A rhizomatous African wetland sedge often grown as an ornamental. Its leafless triangular stems end in a radial umbrella-like whorl of long bracts around clusters of small spikelets. These apparent “leaves” are inflorescence bracts, not ordinary foliage.
Native to tropical and southern Africa, Madagascar and the Arabian Peninsula; naturalised or cultivated widely.
Tufted perennial sedge growing from a creeping rhizome, usually in shallow water or saturated soil.
True leaves are reduced near the stem base; the umbrella blades at each stem tip are involucral bracts.
Numerous small brownish spikelets cluster at the centre of the terminal bracts.
Each flower forms a tiny dry achene enclosed by the glumes of its spikelet.
